questions.q: In Rutherford's scattering experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil. What did this show?

options.A: Most of the atom is empty space.
options.D: Electrons are spread evenly through the atom.

questions.solution: If most alpha particles are not deflected, most of them never come near anything that can push on them. So the atom is mostly empty space. The few that were deflected through large angles showed that the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

questions.q: Which type of radiation passes through paper but is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium?
questions.solution: Beta particles pass through paper but are stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Alpha particles are stopped by paper or a few centimetres of air. Gamma rays are only reduced, by several centimetres of lead.

questions.q: A detector 1.0 m from a small gamma source records 400 counts per second above background. What would it record at 2.0 m?
questions.solution: Gamma radiation spreads out in all directions and is hardly absorbed by air, so its intensity follows an inverse square law. Doubling the distance divides the count rate by four: 400 ÷ 4 = 100 counts per second.

questions.q: A detector near a radioactive source records 425 counts per minute. The background count is 25 counts per minute. What will the detector record after one half-life of the source?
questions.solution: Only the source's own count halves, not the background. The corrected count is 425 − 25 = 400, which falls to 200 after one half-life. The detector still records the background as well: 200 + 25 = 225 counts per minute.

questions.q: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 20 s. What is its decay constant?
questions.solution: \(T_{\frac{1}{2}} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}\), so \(\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{20} = 0.035\ \text{s}^{-1}\). Leaving out \(\ln 2\) (0.050) is the usual slip.

questions.q: A sample contains \(5.0 \times 10^{12}\) nuclei of an isotope with a decay constant of \(2.0 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{s}^{-1}\). What is its activity?
questions.solution: Activity is the number of decays per second: \(A = \lambda N = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 5.0 \times 10^{12} = 1.0 \times 10^{7}\ \text{Bq}\).

questions.q: The graph shows how the activity of a radioactive source falls with time. Its activity is 800 Bq at the start. What is its activity after three half-lives?

figure.alt: Activity against time measured in half-lives: an exponential decay that starts at 800 becquerels and halves in each half-life.

questions.solution: The activity halves in each half-life: 800, 400, 200, then 100 Bq. Three halvings divide it by eight. Dividing by three (267 Bq) is the usual slip.

questions.q: Radioactive decay is described as spontaneous. What does this mean?

options.B: It cannot be predicted which nucleus will decay next.
options.C: It happens to every nucleus at the same moment.
options.D: It is not affected by external conditions such as temperature or pressure.

questions.solution: Spontaneous means the decay is not triggered or changed by anything outside the nucleus: heating, pressure or chemical reactions make no difference. Random is the separate idea that we cannot say which nucleus will decay next, or when.

questions.q: A nucleus has too many neutrons to be stable. How is it most likely to decay?
questions.solution: A neutron-rich nucleus lies above the line of stability. Beta-minus decay turns a neutron into a proton, which moves it towards the line. Proton-rich nuclei decay by beta-plus emission or electron capture, and very heavy nuclei by alpha emission.

questions.q: Nuclear radius is given by \(R = R_{0}A^{\frac{1}{3}}\), with \(R_{0} = 1.2\ \text{fm}\). What is the radius of a nucleus with nucleon number 64?
questions.solution: The cube root of 64 is 4. So the radius is 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 fm. Taking the square root (9.6 fm) or no root at all (77 fm) are the usual slips.

questions.q: How does the density of nuclear matter vary from one nucleus to another?

options.A: It is about the same for all nuclei.
options.B: It is greater for heavier nuclei.
options.C: It is smaller for heavier nuclei.
options.D: It depends on the number of electrons.

questions.solution: The volume of a nucleus is proportional to its radius cubed, and so to its nucleon number. Mass is also proportional to nucleon number. Their ratio, the density, is therefore about the same for every nucleus, and enormously greater than the density of ordinary matter.

questions.q: What is the binding energy of a nucleus?

options.A: The energy needed to remove one electron from the atom.
options.B: The kinetic energy of the nucleons in the nucleus.
options.C: The energy released when the nucleus decays.
options.D: The energy needed to separate the nucleus into its individual nucleons.

questions.solution: Binding energy is the energy needed to pull a nucleus apart into separate protons and neutrons. It equals the mass defect multiplied by the speed of light squared: the nucleus has less mass than its nucleons would have apart.

questions.q: A nuclear reaction has a mass defect of 0.0050 u. How much energy is released? (1 u is equivalent to 931.5 MeV)
questions.solution: Each atomic mass unit of mass defect is equivalent to 931.5 MeV of energy. Energy released = 0.0050 × 931.5 = 4.7 MeV.

questions.q: Which nuclei can release energy by fusing together?
questions.solution: Binding energy per nucleon is greatest near iron. Fusing light nuclei makes a nucleus with more binding energy per nucleon, so energy is released. For nuclei heavier than iron it is splitting, fission, that raises the binding energy per nucleon.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the moderator in a thermal nuclear reactor?

options.A: To absorb neutrons and so control the rate of fission.
options.B: To carry heat away from the core.
options.C: To stop radiation escaping from the reactor.
options.D: To slow down neutrons so that they are more likely to cause fission.

questions.solution: Fission releases fast neutrons, but uranium-235 is far more likely to absorb slow, thermal neutrons. The moderator slows neutrons through repeated collisions. Absorbing neutrons is the job of the control rods, and carrying heat away is the job of the coolant.

questions.q: Why does nuclear fusion need a very high temperature?

options.A: So that nuclei move fast enough to overcome the electrostatic repulsion between them.
options.C: So that electrons can be added to the nuclei.
options.D: So that the strong nuclear force is switched off.

questions.solution: Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. They must get within a few femtometres for the strong nuclear force to pull them together. Only at very high temperature do they have enough kinetic energy to get that close.
